claim: Three separate gerbil families were transferred to an enlarged environment and continuous 20-day audio recordings were obtained.
source: Three separate gerbil families were transferred to an enlarged environment and continuous 20-day audio recordings were obtained.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by experimental methods described in the manuscript.

claim: Using a variational autoencoder (VAE) to quantify 583,237 vocalizations, gerbils exhibit a more elaborate vocal repertoire than has been previously reported.
source: Using a variational autoencoder (VAE) to quantify 583,237 vocalizations, we show that gerbils exhibit a more elaborate vocal repertoire than has been previously reported
evidence: The claim is supported by the VAE analysis of 583,237 vocalizations and discovery of new vocal types shown in Figure 2.

claim: Vocal repertoire usage differs significantly by family.
source: we show that gerbils exhibit a more elaborate vocal repertoire than has been previously reported and that vocal repertoire usage differs significantly by family.
evidence: This is supported by MMD permutation tests and GMM cluster usage analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Families preferentially use characteristic sets of vocal clusters and these usage preferences remain stable over weeks.
source: By performing gaussian mixture model clustering on the VAE latent space, we show that families preferentially use characteristic sets of vocal clusters and that these usage preferences remain stable over weeks.
evidence: This is demonstrated through longitudinal analysis shown in Figure 4, including daily UMAP density plots and PCA projections.

claim: Gerbils displayed family-specific transitions between vocal clusters.
source: Furthermore, gerbils displayed family-specific transitions between vocal clusters.
evidence: This is supported by transition matrix analysis and bigram probability graphs shown in Figure 5.

claim: Gerbils live naturally as extended families in complex underground burrows that are adjacent to other families.
source: Since gerbils live naturally as extended families in complex underground burrows that are adjacent to other families
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature on gerbil natural behavior.

claim: The presence of a vocal dialect could be exploited by animals to represent kinship.
source: these results suggest the presence of a vocal dialect which could be exploited by animals to represent kinship.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the family-specific vocal usage patterns observed in the data.

claim: 10,267,972 sound events were extracted, containing 583,237 vocalizations and 9,684,735 non-vocal sounds detected across the three families.
source: Using this approach, 10,267,972 sound events were extracted, containing 583,237 vocalizations and 9,684,735 non-vocal sounds detected across the three families.
evidence: This is a direct report of the data extraction results from the audio recordings.

claim: Sound events were produced at an average rate of 6726+/-1260 times per hour.
source: Sound events were produced at an average rate of 6726+/-1260 times per hour (Figure 1D)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Vocalizations represent 6.99+/-3.07% of all sound events over the recording period.
source: Vocalizations represent 6.99+/-3.07% of all sound events over the recording period (Figure 1E)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Vocalizations were emitted at an average rate of 405+/-103 times per hour.
source: were emitted at an average rate of 405+/-103 times per hour (Figure 1F)
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A threshold value of 0.3 for spectral flatness minimized the number of false positives in vocalization detection.
source: A similar approach has previously been used in mice (Castellucci et al., 2016), and we verified that a threshold value of 0.3 minimized the number of false positives (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by empirical validation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citation to prior work.

claim: The gerbil vocal repertoire is more discrete than mouse, yet less discrete than zebra finch.
source: Figure 2B shows a UMAP embedding of the VAE latents (center), used for visualization purposes only, which demonstrates that the gerbil vocal repertoire is more discrete than mouse, yet less discrete than zebra finch (Sainburg et al., 2020; Goffinet et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparative inference based on UMAP visualization and citations to prior work on mouse and zebra finch.

claim: Vocalizations occur as either single syllables bounded by silence (monosyllabic) or consist of combinations of single syllables without a silent interval (multisyllabic).
source: Vocalizations occur as either single syllables bounded by silence (monosyllabic) or consist of combinations of single syllables without a silent interval (multisyllabic).
evidence: This is a descriptive categorization of the vocalizations observed in the data.

claim: Monosyllabic vocalizations account for 56 out of 70 vocal clusters.
source: Furthermore, monosyllabic vocalizations (56/70 vocal clusters) can be flexibly strung together to create multisyllabic or 'composite' vocalizations (9/70 of vocal clusters; Kobayasi and Riquimaroux, 2012).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the cluster composition with citation to prior work.

claim: Multisyllabic vocalizations account for 9 out of 70 vocal clusters.
source: Furthermore, monosyllabic vocalizations (56/70 vocal clusters) can be flexibly strung together to create multisyllabic or 'composite' vocalizations (9/70 of vocal clusters; Kobayasi and Riquimaroux, 2012).
evidence: This is a quantitative description of the cluster composition with citation to prior work.

claim: One vocalization appears similar in form to naked mole rat family specific chirp.
source: Representative examples from 12 monosyllabic vocalization clusters are shown with their relative position in UMAP space, one of which appears similar in form to naked mole rat family specific chirp (blue box with asterisk; Barker et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparative observation based on visual similarity with citation to prior work on naked mole rats.

claim: Pup weaning causes a drastic decrease in vocal emission.
source: To assess how family structure influences vocal repertoire usage, we compared vocal usage one day prior and one day after pup weaning, showing a drastic decrease in vocal emission (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data comparing pre- and post-weaning vocal emission.

claim: A large-magnitude vocal repertoire change is observed following weaning, with the repertoire confined to a small region of vocal space.
source: A large-magnitude vocal repertoire change is also observed, with the repertoire confined to a small region of vocal space following weaning (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data comparing pre- and post-weaning vocal repertoire.

claim: All families used each of the 70 vocal types (i.e. no cluster usage is 0).
source: All families used each of the 70 vocal types (i.e. no cluster usage is 0), but each family relied more heavily on some clusters as compared to others.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the GMM cluster usage analysis.

claim: Each family relied more heavily on some clusters as compared to others.
source: All families used each of the 70 vocal types (i.e. no cluster usage is 0), but each family relied more heavily on some clusters as compared to others.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the GMM cluster usage analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The general finding of family-specific vocal usage was robust across a wide range of GMM clusters.
source: Although we chose 70 clusters for our analyses, the general finding was robust across a wide range of GMM clusters (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Families overexpress dissimilar vocal clusters relative to each other.
source: Families overexpress dissimilar vocal clusters relative to each other (e.g. clusters 4 and 8 in Family 2) and similar vocal clusters relative to each other (e.g. cluster 14 in Family 1 and cluster 1 in Family 3; cluster 9 in Family 1 and cluster 5 in Family 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the differential cluster usage analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Families overexpress similar vocal clusters relative to each other.
source: Families overexpress dissimilar vocal clusters relative to each other (e.g. clusters 4 and 8 in Family 2) and similar vocal clusters relative to each other (e.g. cluster 14 in Family 1 and cluster 1 in Family 3; cluster 9 in Family 1 and cluster 5 in Family 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the differential cluster usage analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The density map of vocal usage remains coarsely stable across days within families.
source: There are two noteworthy trends: (1) the density map remains coarsely stable across days (rows) and (2) the maps look distinct across families on any given day (columns).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the daily UMAP density plots shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The vocal usage maps look distinct across families on any given day.
source: There are two noteworthy trends: (1) the density map remains coarsely stable across days (rows) and (2) the maps look distinct across families on any given day (columns).
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the daily UMAP density plots shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cluster usages are stable across days within families during the period of 'full family, shared recording days'.
source: Cluster usages during the period of 'full family, shared recording days' (postnatal days beneath the purple bars) are stable across days within families – as is apparent by the horizontal striations in the plot – although each family maintains this stability through using a unique set of call types.
evidence: This is an observation from the daily cluster usage analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Each family maintains stability through using a unique set of call types.
source: Cluster usages during the period of 'full family, shared recording days' (postnatal days beneath the purple bars) are stable across days within families – as is apparent by the horizontal striations in the plot – although each family maintains this stability through using a unique set of call types.
evidence: This is an observation from the daily cluster usage analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PCA projections of cluster usages show clearly separable families.
source: This is addressed empirically in Figure 4C, which shows clearly separable PCA projections of the cluster usages shown in Figure 4B (purple days, concatenated into a 45 day x 70 cluster matrix).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the PCA analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Across-family repertoire differences are substantially larger than within-family differences.
source: Finally, we computed the pairwise Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) between latent distributions of vocalizations from individual recording days for each of the families (Figure 4D). This shows that across-family repertoire differences are substantially larger than within-family differences.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the MMD analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Vocal emission follows a diurnal activity pattern that was similar across the three families recorded.
source: First, we summed the total vocal emission for each hour of the day over the entire recording period, which revealed a diurnal activity pattern that was similar across the three families recorded (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the hourly vocal emission analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The majority of vocalizations occurred in bouts (58.5±0.9%).
source: The majority of vocalizations occurred in bouts (58.5±0.9%), which we extracted using two criteria: (1) vocalizations within a bout display inter-vocalization-interval of <2 s, and (2) a bout contains at least 5 vocalizations (based on Rose et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the data with citation to prior work for the bout definition criteria.

claim: The distribution of bout durations, inter-vocalization-intervals, and vocalization durations for each family are highly overlapping and contain the same peaks.
source: The distribution of bout durations, inter-vocalization-intervals, and vocalization durations for each family are highly overlapping and contain the same peaks (Figure 5B–D), suggesting that the temporal structure of vocal emission does not vary by family.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the temporal analysis shown in Figure 5B-D.

claim: The temporal structure of vocal emission does not vary by family.
source: The distribution of bout durations, inter-vocalization-intervals, and vocalization durations for each family are highly overlapping and contain the same peaks (Figure 5B–D), suggesting that the temporal structure of vocal emission does not vary by family.
evidence: This is an inference from the overlapping distributions of temporal features across families.

claim: Vocalization bouts show striking structure in vocal type sequencing.
source: Vocalization bouts show striking structure in vocal type sequencing (Figure 5E, F)
evidence: This is a qualitative observation from the bout examples shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: Vocal cluster transition matrices revealed a strong self-transition preference for all vocal clusters across families.
source: Vocal cluster transition matrices revealed a strong self-transition preference for all vocal clusters across families (Figure 5G)
evidence: This is a direct observation from the transition matrix analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The proportion usage of different transitions (including self-transitions) drastically varied by family.
source: however, the proportion usage of different transitions (including self-transitions) drastically varied by family (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is a direct observation from the bigram probability graph shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Most transitions for each family occur significantly above chance levels.
source: As is made clear in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, most transitions for each family occur significantly above chance levels, despite the inherent 1 gram structure.
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing using shuffled null distributions shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Families arrange the same sets of vocal clusters into unique sequences.
source: Moreover, by looking at transitions from a highly usage cluster type used roughly the same proportion across families (cluster 12), we show that families arrange the same sets of vocal clusters into unique sequences (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the transition analysis from cluster 12 shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Natural observations are often incomplete due to limitations in physical access for experimenter observation or behavioral recording.
source: However, natural observations are often incomplete due to limitations in physical access for experimenter observation or behavioral recording.
evidence: This is a general statement about limitations in ethological research based on established knowledge.

claim: Limitations in observation can be particularly severe for family behaviors which occur in protected or remote environments, such as burrows in the case of fossorial rodent species like naked mole-rats and Mongolian gerbils.
source: This can be particularly severe for family behaviors which occur in protected or remote environments, such as burrows in the case of fossorial rodent species like naked mole-rats and Mongolian gerbils (Brett, 1986; Scheibler et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on fossorial rodent behavior.

claim: Some limitations in natural observation have been addressed with laboratory environments that partially recapitulate real-world features.
source: Some of these limitations have been addressed with laboratory environments that partially recapitulate real-world features (Shemesh and Chen, 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work on naturalistic laboratory environments.

claim: Laboratory studies generally focused on relatively short periods of data collection that consider single animals or dyads with no prior social relationship.
source: However, these studies generally focused on relatively short periods of data collection that consider single animals or dyads with no prior social relationship.
evidence: This is a general characterization of prior laboratory studies based on knowledge of the field.

claim: Many vocal cues are learned through social experience, and provide pivotal information about an animal's identity.
source: we know that many vocal cues are learned through social experience, and provide pivotal information about an animal's identity.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations to follow.

claim: A human infant's ability to discriminate between foreign language phonemes can be preserved by exposure to a live foreign speaker, but not an audiovisual recording.
source: For example, a human infant's ability to discriminate between foreign language phonemes can be preserved by exposure to a live foreign speaker, but not an audiovisual recording (Kuhl et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on human infant language learning.

claim: Evidence from swamp sparrows suggests the presence of culturally transmissible 'dialects'.
source: Evidence from swamp sparrows suggests the presence of culturally transmissible 'dialects' – a term borrowed from linguistics to denote a pattern of vocal behavior that is used by members of a social group (Maler and Tamura, 1964).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on swamp sparrow vocal behavior.

claim: Naked mole rats learn colony-specific dialects based on early social experience.
source: Even some rodents, such as the naked mole rat, learn colony-specific dialects based on early social experience (Barker et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on naked mole rat vocal learning.

claim: The literature for social facilitation of vocal discrimination or production is particularly strong for zebra finches.
source: The literature for social facilitation of vocal discrimination or production is particularly strong for zebra finches (Eales, 1989; Derégnaucourt et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2016; Narula et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on zebra finch vocal learning.

claim: Gerbils form pair bonds and maintain a family structure across generations.
source: Unlike many laboratory rodents, gerbils form pair bonds and maintain a family structure across generations (Ågren, 1984a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on gerbil social structure.

claim: Gerbil families are composed of a founding adult pair, and up to 15 extended family members that live cooperatively in underground burrows.
source: These families are composed of a founding adult pair, and up to 15 extended family members that live cooperatively in underground burrows (Ågren et al., 1989a; Ågren et al., 1989b; Milne-Edwards, 1867; Scheibler et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on gerbil family structure and natural behavior.

claim: Gerbils are thought to rely heavily on their auditory system for social interactions given the darkness and complexity of their burrow systems.
source: Given the darkness and complexity of their burrow systems, gerbils are thought to rely heavily on their auditory system for social interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ecological constraints of burrow living.

claim: Sibling bonds established through adolescence facilitate social structure and minimize inbreeding.
source: Sibling bonds established through adolescence facilitate social structure and minimize inbreeding (Ågren, 1984b).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on gerbil social development.

claim: Natural burrows are found in multi-family neighborhoods with strictly enforced territorial boundaries.
source: Natural burrows are found in multi-family neighborhoods with strictly enforced territorial boundaries (Scheibler et al., 2006; Ågren et al., 1989a; Ågren et al., 1989b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on gerbil territorial behavior.

claim: Gerbils act cooperatively to hoard food, maintain nests, defend their territory, and care for pups.
source: Like prairie voles, gerbils act cooperatively to hoard food, maintain nests, defend their territory, and care for pups (Elwood, 1975; Gromov, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on gerbil cooperative behavior.

claim: Gerbils display significant vocal communication in both the ultrasonic and sonic ranges.
source: Gerbils also display significant vocal communication in both the ultrasonic and sonic ranges (Rübsamen et al., 2012; Kobayasi and Riquimaroux, 2012) which is likely to be integral to social behaviors.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on gerbil vocalizations.

claim: Unlike many other rodent species, gerbils are able to hear within sonic ranges at sensitivities similar to humans.
source: Unlike many other rodent species, gerbils are able to hear within sonic ranges at sensitivities similar to humans (Ryan, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on gerbil auditory sensitivity.

claim: Continuous recordings began at P11-13 when auditory cortex is particularly sensitive to acoustic experience.
source: Specifically, we recorded audio over a period beginning at postnatal day 11–13 when auditory cortex is particularly sensitive to acoustic experience, and extending to postnatal day 31–32, the time when animals are typically weaned.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about auditory cortex critical periods.

claim: Recordings extended to postnatal day 31–32, the time when animals are typically weaned.
source: Specifically, we recorded audio over a period beginning at postnatal day 11–13 when auditory cortex is particularly sensitive to acoustic experience, and extending to postnatal day 31–32, the time when animals are typically weaned.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about gerbil weaning age.

claim: The VAE learned a low-dimensional representation of latent acoustic features, enabling analysis of a large dataset with larger representational capacity than standard acoustic features.
source: The VAE learned a low-dimensional representation of latent acoustic features, thereby enabling analysis of such a large dataset with a larger representational capacity than standard acoustic features (Goffinet et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on VAE methods for vocalization analysis.

claim: 70 vocal clusters were selected as a parsimonious description of the data using a combination of the elbow method on held-out log likelihood and established knowledge for how many vocal types gerbils emit.
source: Using a combination of the elbow method on held-out log likelihood and established knowledge for how many vocal types gerbils emit (see Methods, GMM clustering), we selected a model with 70 vocal clusters as a parsimonious description of the data (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is based on both data-driven model selection and prior knowledge about gerbil vocal repertoire.

claim: Female macaques learn to recognize the vocalizations of their own offspring during the second postnatal week, and retain this ability for at least 6 months.
source: For example, female macaques learn to recognize the vocalizations of their own offspring during the second postnatal week, and retain this ability for at least 6 months (Jovanovic et al., 2000; Shizawa et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on macaque vocal recognition.

claim: Kittens learn their mother's vocalizations, and Australian sea lions can recall their mother's voice up to 2 years after weaning.
source: Similarly, kittens learn their mother's vocalizations, and Australian sea lions can recall their mother's voice up to 2 years after weaning (Pitcher et al., 2010; Szenczi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on vocal recognition in kittens and sea lions.

claim: When exposed to a chicken maternal call during development, socially reared mallard ducklings come to prefer it over their own species' call.
source: For example, when exposed to a chicken maternal call during development, socially reared mallard ducklings come to prefer it over their own species' call (Gottlieb, 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on mallard duckling vocal learning.

claim: Wood ducklings must be exposed to sibling vocalizations in order to remain selectively responsive to its mother's assembly call.
source: Similarly, wood ducklings must be exposed to sibling vocalizations in order to remain selectively responsive to its mother's assembly call (Gottlieb, 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on wood duckling vocal development.

claim: Horseshoe bats, naked mole rats, and dolphins each model their calls based on early social experience.
source: Horseshoe bats, naked mole rats, and dolphins each model their calls based on early social experience (Jones and Ransome, 1993; Fripp et al., 2005; Favaro et al., 2016; Barker et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work on vocal learning in these species.

claim: Rodent vocalizations can harbor information about the individual identity and colony membership of the vocalizer.
source: Finally, rodent vocalizations can also harbor information about the individual identity and colony membership of the vocalizer (Barker et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on rodent vocal identity.

claim: Exposure to a live singing tutor, but not song playback, selectively activates dopamine neurons in the juvenile periaqueductal gray which is thought to mediate learning in zebra finches.
source: In fact, research on song learning in zebra finches shows that a reward learning mechanism may support the transmission of vocal repertoires: exposure to a live singing tutor, but not song playback, selectively activates dopamine neurons in the juvenile periaqueductal gray which is thought to mediate learning (Tanaka et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on zebra finch neural mechanisms of vocal learning.

claim: The differences in vocal usage align with the definition of human vocal dialect, which is a regional or social variety of language that can differ in pronunciation, grammatical, semantic and/or language use differences.
source: The differences in this study align with the definition of human vocal dialect, which is a regional or social variety of language that can differ in pronunciation, grammatical, semantic and/or language use differences (Henry et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a conceptual alignment with the linguistic definition of dialect, supported by citation.

claim: Vocal clusters can be rarely observed in some families yet highly overexpressed in others (analogous to language usage differences in humans).
source: In our case, vocal clusters can be rarely observed in some families yet highly overexpressed in others (e.g. analogous to language usage differences in humans)
evidence: This is an observation from the data with an analogy to human language usage.

claim: Vocal clusters can be highly expressed in both families, but contain subtle spectrotemporal variations (analogous to pronunciation differences in humans).
source: or highly expressed in both families, but contain subtle spectrotemporal variations (Figure 3D, Family 1 cluster 11 vs. Family 3 clusters 2, 18, 30; for example analogous to pronunciation differences in humans).
evidence: This is an observation from the data with an analogy to human pronunciation differences.

claim: It is possible that gerbils may possess the ability to acquire family specific vocal behavior through experience, like naked mole-rats.
source: Like another fossorial species, the naked mole-rat, it is possible that gerbils may also possess the ability to acquire family specific vocal behavior through experience (Barker et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on comparison to naked mole-rats, supported by citation.

claim: Unlike the naked mole-rat which showed the presence of a colony-specific vocal dialect in a single vocal type (the soft chirp), gerbils show that fine spectrotemporal variations in multiple different vocal types could harbor dialects.
source: Unlike the naked mole-rat which showed the presence of a colony-specific vocal dialect in a single vocal type, the soft chirp, we show that fine spectrotemporal variations in multiple different gerbil vocal types could harbor dialects (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a comparative inference based on the data and prior work on naked mole-rats.

claim: Vocalization emission statistics and behavioral syllable transition patterns can signify differences between groups of animals.
source: Vocalization emission statistics and behavioral syllable transition patterns can signify differences between groups of animals (Castellucci et al., 2018; Wiltschko et al., 2015; Markowitz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on vocal and behavioral patterns.

claim: Vocal emission follows a diurnal pattern, with peaks of activity in the morning and afternoon.
source: First, we observed that vocal emission follows a diurnal pattern, with peaks of activity in the morning and afternoon.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the hourly vocal emission analysis.

claim: Prior work in gerbils showed diurnal activity patterns in gerbil groups for non-vocal behaviors.
source: This result complements prior work in gerbils showing diurnal activity patterns in gerbil groups for non-vocal behaviors (Pietrewicz et al., 1982), but extends our understanding to vocal behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on gerbil activity patterns.

claim: Vocalizations are rarely emitted in isolation but rather in sequences ('bouts') with a modal duration of 4 s.
source: Vocalizations are rarely emitted in isolation. Rather, they are emitted in sequences ('bouts') with a modal duration of 4 s and a duration distribution that does not vary between families.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the bout duration analysis.

claim: The bout emission statistics are somewhat consistent with the common phoneme rate in humans.
source: These emission statistics are somewhat consistent with the common phoneme rate in humans (Edwards and Chang, 2013; Ding et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a comparative inference supported by citations to prior work on human speech rates.

claim: A fully realized assessment of vocalization usage should be integrated with continuous sub-second synchronized videographic data from which one can extract animal pose estimation and behavioral categorization.
source: First, a fully realized assessment of vocalization usage should be integrated with continuous sub-second synchronized videographic data from which one can extract animal pose estimation and behavioral categorization.
evidence: This is a discussion of study limitations and future directions.

claim: Videographic data could allow control for the total number and type of social interactions, which may explain differences in the amount or usage of specific syllables.
source: For example, such data could allow us to control for the total number and type of social interactions, which may explain differences in the amount or usage of specific syllables.
evidence: This is a speculative discussion of how additional data could inform interpretation.

claim: It was not possible to localize the majority of vocalizations with sufficient spatial resolution using Mouse Ultrasonic Source Estimation software.
source: Second, although we used four microphones, it was not possible to localize the majority of vocalizations with sufficient spatial resolution (using Mouse Ultrasonic Source Estimation software; Neunuebel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about a technical limitation of the study with citation to the software used.

claim: To properly address whether individual animals emit a unique vocalization repertoire, significant advances in the field of computational bioacoustics will be required.
source: To properly address whether individual animals emit a unique vocalization repertoire, we will require significant advances in the field of computational bioacoustics.
evidence: This is a discussion of current limitations and future needs in the field.

claim: The sudden reduction of sonic calls following pup removal could suggest that these vocalizations are produced selectively by pups.
source: The results show a clear effect of family integrity, and the sudden reduction of sonic calls following pup removal (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) could suggest that these vocalizations are produced selectively by pups.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the weaning data.

claim: There is ample evidence that adult gerbils also produce sonic vocalizations.
source: However, there is ample evidence that adult gerbils also produce sonic vocalizations.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from prior literature.

claim: A number of low-frequency call types are used by adults during a range of social interactions.
source: For example, a number of low-frequency call types are used by adults during a range of social interactions (Rübsamen et al., 2012; Furuyama et al., 2022), some of which are similar to a low-frequency call type used by pups (Silberstein et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on adult gerbil vocalizations.

claim: When gerbil pups are recorded during isolation, ultrasonic vocalization rate declines and sonic vocalizations increase for animals that are in a high arousal state.
source: Thus, when gerbil pups are recorded during isolation, ultrasonic vocalization rate declines and sonic vocalizations increase for animals that are in a high arousal state (De Ghett, 1974; Silberstein et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on gerbil pup vocalizations during isolation.

claim: As gerbils progress from juvenile to adolescent development (P17-55) a significant increase in ultrasonic vocalization rate is observed during dyadic social encounters, with a distinct change in usage pattern that depends upon the sex of each animal.
source: As gerbils progress from juvenile to adolescent development (P17-55) a significant increase in ultrasonic vocalization rate is observed during dyadic social encounters, with a distinct change in usage pattern that depends upon the sex of each animal (Holman and Seale, 1991; Holman et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on gerbil vocal development.

claim: In fat-tailed gerbils, the number of ultrasonic vocalization syllable types increase from neonatal to adult animals.
source: The development of vocalization types has been assessed in another member of the Gerbillinae subfamily, called fat-tailed gerbils (Pachyuromys duprasi), during isolation and handling. Here, the number of ultrasonic vocalization syllable types increase from neonatal to adult animals (Zaytseva et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on fat-tailed gerbil vocal development.

claim: In fat-tailed gerbils, some very low frequency sonic call types were rarely observed after P20.
source: while some very low frequency sonic call types were rarely observed after P20 (Zaytseva et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on fat-tailed gerbil vocal development.

claim: In mice, syllable usage changes during development, but pups produced 10 of the 11 syllable types produced by adults.
source: By comparison, mouse syllable usage changes during development, but pups produced 10 of the 11 syllable types produced by adults (Grimsley et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on mouse vocal development.

claim: When recorded in their natural environment, chimpanzees display a prolonged maturation of vocalization complexity, such as the probability of a unique utterance in a sequence, with the greatest changes occurring when animals begin to experience non-kin social interactions.
source: For example, when recorded in their natural environment, chimpanzees display a prolonged maturation of vocalization complexity, such as the probability of a unique utterance in a sequence, with the greatest changes occuring when animals begin to experience non-kin social interactions (Bortolato et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on chimpanzee vocal development.

claim: Long-term behavioral monitoring of a core social unit (the family) reveals richer vocal behavior than has previously been reported in the gerbil species.
source: Our findings indicate that long-term behavioral monitoring of a core social unit (i.e. the family) reveals richer vocal behavior than has previously been reported in the species.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in the study.

claim: These findings establish the Mongolian gerbil as a useful model organism for studying the neurobiology of vocal interactions in complex social groups.
source: Taken together, these findings establish the Mongolian gerbil as a useful model organism for studying the neurobiology of vocal interactions in complex social groups.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the implications of the findings.

claim: Three gerbil families (Meriones unguiculatus, n=6 per family: 2 adults, 4 pups) were used in this study.
source: Three gerbil families (Meriones unguiculatus, n=6 per family: 2 adults, 4 pups) were used in this study (Charles River).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental subjects used.

claim: All procedures related to the maintenance and use of animals were approved by the University Animal Welfare Committee at New York University (protocol 2020–1112).
source: All procedures related to the maintenance and use of animals were approved by the University Animal Welfare Committee at New York University (protocol 2020–1112), and all experiments were performed in accordance with the relevant guidelines and regulations.
evidence: This is a statement of ethical approval for the study.

claim: Four ultrasonic microphones were synchronously recorded using a National Instruments multifunction data acquisition device at a 125 kHz sampling rate.
source: Four ultrasonic microphones (Avisoft CM16/CMPA48AAF-5V) were synchronously recorded using a National Instruments multifunction data acquisition device (PCI-6143) via BNC connection with a National Instruments terminal block (BNC-2110). The recording was controlled with custom python scripts using the NI-DAQmx-python library version 0.5.7; (https://github.com/ni/nidaqmx-python; National Instruments, 2017) which wrote samples to disk at a 125 kHz sampling rate.
evidence: This is a description of the recording methods used in the study.

claim: In total, 13.084 TB of raw audio data were acquired across the three families.
source: In total, 13.084 TB of raw audio data were acquired across the three families.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the data volume collected.

claim: Audio was segmented by amplitude thresholding using the Autoencoded Vocal Analysis (AVA) python package.
source: Audio was segmented by amplitude thresholding using the Autoencoded Vocal Analysis (AVA) python package (see Goffinet et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the audio segmentation method with citation to the software package.

claim: The maximum and minimum syllable durations were selected based on published duration ranges of gerbil vocalizations.
source: The maximum and minimum syllable durations were selected based on published duration ranges of gerbil vocalizations (Rübsamen et al., 2012; Kobayasi and Riquimaroux, 2012).
evidence: This is a methodological choice based on prior literature, supported by citations.

claim: Spectral flatness was computed using the python package librosa.
source: We computed the spectral flatness of each detected sound event using the python package librosa (https://github.com/librosa; McFee et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a description of the computational method used with citation to the software.

claim: A spectral flatness threshold of 0.3 was used to separate putative vocal and non-vocal sounds, consistent with prior literature.
source: Consistent with prior literature (Castellucci et al., 2016), we used a threshold on spectral flatness to separate putative vocal and non-vocal sounds.
evidence: This is a methodological choice consistent with prior work, supported by citation.

claim: The spectral flatness threshold of 0.3 had a 5.5+/-1.96% false positive rate.
source: We quantified the false positive vocalization rate for each threshold value and selected 0.3, which had a 5.5+/-1.96% false positive rate.
evidence: This is a quantitative validation of the threshold selection.

claim: A VAE was trained for 50 epochs using a model precision of 40.
source: A VAE was trained for 50 epochs using a model precision of 40.
evidence: This is a description of the VAE training parameters.

claim: GMMs were fit to cluster VAE latent feature vectors using 7 of 32 VAE latents, which explained 99.5% of the variance in the original feature space.
source: GMMs were fit to cluster VAE latent feature vectors. To reduce computation time, we fit the model on 7 of 32 VAE latents (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), as these explained 99.5% of the variance in the original feature space.
evidence: This is a description of the GMM fitting procedure with justification for dimensionality reduction.

claim: The GMM model was implemented in Stan and fit using stochastic variational inference.
source: The model was implemented in Stan (https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanpy), however similar clustering results were achieved using the scikit-learn Gaussian Mixture model class with a diagonal covariance matrix (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.mixture.GaussianMixture.html). We fit the model using stochastic variational inference, an approximate Bayesian inference technique that recasts the task of learning a posterior distribution as an optimization problem and enables vast speedups (Hoffman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical modeling approach with citation to the method.

claim: The GMM was modified to allow, although not enforce, the model to learn different cluster usage patterns for each family.
source: GMMs typically assume that the whole population selects clusters with the same probabilities, however we modified this assumption to allow, although not enforce, the model to learn different cluster usage patterns for each family.
evidence: This is a description of a methodological modification to the standard GMM approach.

claim: Previous work documenting the Mongolian gerbil repertoire has revealed ~12 vocalization types that vary with social context.
source: Previous work documenting the Mongolian gerbil repertoire (Rübsamen et al., 2012; Kobayasi and Riquimaroux, 2012) has revealed ~12 vocalization types that vary with social context.
evidence: This is a summary of prior literature on gerbil vocal repertoire, supported by citations.

claim: It is likely that the 70 clusters capture the ~12 known vocalization types plus individual or family-specific variations of some call types.
source: It is likely that we are capturing these ~12 (plus a few more, as illustrated in Figure 2C) as well as individual or family-specific variations of some call types.
evidence: This is an interpretation of why the number of clusters exceeds the number of known call types.

claim: It is plausible that variation due to vocalizer identity pushes some calls into unique clusters.
source: Although the number of discrete call types is likely less than 70, it is plausible that variation due to vocalizer identity pushes some calls into unique clusters.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the number of clusters observed.

claim: Both naked mole rats and Mongolian gerbils have been shown to exhibit individual-specific variation in vocalizations, though only in single call types.
source: This idea is supported by the fact that both naked mole rats and Mongolian gerbils have been shown to exhibit individual-specific variation in vocalizations, though only in single call types (Figure 1 from Barker et al., 2021; Table I from Nishiyama et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on individual vocal variation in these species.

claim: Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) was used to quantify the difference between two latent distributions of vocalizations.
source: Specifically, we used Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) to quantify the difference between two latent distributions of vocalizations.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical method used for distribution comparison.

claim: MMD considers two sets of observed data points which are assumed to be independent and identically distributed random variables from underlying probability distributions, and returns a distance metric corresponding to the equality of the two distributions.
source: This test considers two sets of observed data points (e.g. N vocalizations from Family 1 and N vocalizations from Family 2), which are assumed to be independent and identically distributed random variables from underlying probability distributions, and returns a distance metric corresponding to the equality of the two distributions (Gretton et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the MMD method with citation to the original work.

claim: The empirically observed MMD2 distances were much higher than the shuffle control, favoring the alternative hypothesis that gerbil families utilize distinct syllable usage statistics.
source: The empirically observed MMD2 distances were much higher than the shuffle control, favoring the alternative hypothesis that gerbil families utilize distinct syllable usage statistics (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the MMD permutation test.

claim: Vocalization transition sequences were generated by concatenating vocal cluster labels chronologically for each family.
source: Vocalization transition sequences were generated by concatenating vocal cluster labels chronologically for each family and calculating the number of transitions for all possible transition types.
evidence: This is a description of the transition analysis method.

claim: Vocal cluster label sequences were randomly shuffled 1000 times independently for each family to generate a null transition matrix distribution.
source: We randomly shuffled label sequences 1000 times independently for each family to generate a null transition matrix distribution.
evidence: This is a description of the statistical control procedure for transition analysis.

claim: A p-value for each transition was computed using a one-sample t-test with post hoc Benjamini-Hochberg multiple comparisons correction.
source: Using these null distributions and the observed transition probabilities, we computed a p-value for each transition using a one-sample t-test and created a binary transition matrix indicating which transitions happen above chance levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C, black pixels, P ≤ 0.05 after post hoc Benjamini-Hochberg multiple comparisons correction).
evidence: This is a description of the statistical testing procedure for transitions.

claim: Acoustic features were calculated using the VocalPy 'similarity_features' function, a python implementation of the Sound Analysis Pro Sound Analysis Tools library.
source: Next, using the VocalPy (Nicholson, 2023) 'similarity_features' function (a python implementation of the Sound Analysis Pro Sound Analysis Tools library: http://soundanalysispro.com/matlab-sat), the following acoustic features were calculated: fundamental frequency (pitch), amplitude, entropy, frequency modulation, goodness of pitch.
evidence: This is a description of the acoustic feature calculation method with citation to the software.
